# A "Conversion Phase" Does Not Convert Strength Into Power: Maximal Strength Is a Foundation, Not a Raw Material

**What it is** — "Some authorities consider that one of the transition phases should be recognised as a *conversion phase* during which specialised training converts maximum strength either into speed-strength or strength-endurance. Although this terminology superficially seems attractive and descriptive, it is scientifically inaccurate, since one type of strength or motor ability cannot change into another, as has been shown by considerable research into the specificity of adaptation. It is more accurate to state that a prior stage of maximal strength training may serve as the *foundation* upon which later training for speed-strength or endurance is based, a sequence which is fundamental to some systems of training, e.g. the conjugate sequence system (see 5.3)" (PDF p. 327 / printed p. 316, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the specificity of adaptation; they cite "considerable research" without naming studies on this page. Inference: the practical difference is that a "foundation" view expects the later speed-strength phase to need its own specific training stimulus, whereas "conversion" implies the strength gained is transformed by the later phase.

**When to apply** — When writing or reviewing a block sequence that labels a phase "conversion" or "strength to power." Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)). The authors would accept that sequence but describe the strength block as a foundation for the strength-to-power block, not as something the later block converts.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and framing correction; the authors do not say the sequence itself is wrong, and they endorse it within the conjugate sequence system. The passage gives no data, so it does not settle how much maximal strength work must precede speed-strength work.

**Example** — The authors' own pointer: in the conjugate sequence system's speed-strength sequence, concentrated strength loading is followed by technique work "against a background of the delayed training effect of the strength block" (Section 5.3.3, PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293; see [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]).

**Related** — [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]], [[framework--training-cycle-hierarchy-durations-and-russian-term-swap]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]

# Matveyev's Microcycle and Mesocycle Types, and How Sequences of Them Build a Phase

**What it is** — Following Matveyev (1981), the authors list microcycle types (PDF p. 327-328 / printed p. 316-317, verified against the page images): *ordinary* ("the usual scheme of uniformly increasing loading"), *introductory* ("bringing the athlete up to the competition stage"), *restorative* ("after heavy loading"), *competitive* ("immediately before and including the competition") and *shock* or stress ("stimulating the athlete out of a state of stagnation"). Sample mesocycles built from them:
- ordinary > ordinary > shock > restorative
- ordinary > introductory > competitive > restorative
- shock > ordinary > shock > restorative
- restorative > ordinary > ordinary > restorative

Mesocycle types (Matveyev, 1981): *introductory* (beginning the preparatory period), *base* ("the main types for increasing specific functional abilities"), *control-preparatory* (between base and competitive), *pre-competitive*, *competitive*, and *intermediate* (restorative), the last sometimes split into restorative-preparatory and restorative-maintenance; the latter "is simply referred to as a maintenance phase." "Large mesocycles" are integrated systems of smaller ones. A phase is a sequence of mesocycles (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317):
- Long-duration endurance, preparatory phase: introductory > base (general preparatory, developing) > base (stabilising) > base (special preparatory, developing) > control-preparatory > base > pre-competitive.
- Speed-strength, two options: introductory > base (developing > control-preparatory) > base (with pre-competitive elements); or introductory > base (general preparatory) > base (special preparatory) > pre-competitive.

**Why it works** — Classification, not mechanism. The authors give each type its purpose (above); the restorative and intermediate types exist to "help the athlete recover after heavy loading" through "systematic active rest" (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317).

**When to apply** — As a vocabulary for writing a mesocycle as a string of purposeful weeks rather than a single load trend. Eric's baseline: "The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: in Matveyev's terms each football game week is a competitive microcycle, and a bye week (line 187) plays the role of a short intermediate or restorative unit with a top-up.

**When NOT to apply** — The "ordinary" microcycle is defined as "uniformly increasing loading," which sits uneasily with the authors' own recommendation to alternate light, medium and heavy loading (PDF p. 326, 329; see [[claim--heavy-medium-light-alternation-beats-monotonic-increasing-loading]]); Inference: read "ordinary" as the default building week, not as a recommendation for monotonic loading. Section 6.3 reports critics of "the artificiality and clumsiness of classifying the various microcycles and mesocycles" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). Issurin's microcycle typology differs in names and in its load-wave detail ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); do not mix the two vocabularies without saying which is meant.

**Example** — The authors' own: a mesocycle of ordinary > ordinary > shock > restorative microcycles (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317).

**Related** — [[heuristic--shock-microcycle-limits]], [[framework--training-cycle-hierarchy-durations-and-russian-term-swap]], [[principle--sporting-form-cannot-be-held-permanently-matveyev]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]

- ordinary > introductory > competitive > restorative
- shock > ordinary > shock > restorative

# GPP and SPP Form One Unit: Use SPP Work Inside GPP When Needed, and Curtail Standard GPP for Advanced Athletes

**What it is** — The preparatory phase splits into GPP (General Physical Preparation) and SPP (Specialised Physical Preparation), but "the GPP and SPP always form an interconnected unit. In some cases, the GPP and SPP may even be concurrent or the GPP may be largely indistinguishable from the SPP (Bondarchuk, 1979)" (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317, verified against the page image). GPP gives "balanced physical conditioning in endurance, strength, speed, flexibility and other basic factors," often through varied low-intensity activities (jogging, swimming, cycling, tennis, volleyball); it is the time to gain muscle or lose excess fat, and "an *hypertrophy phase* may be included" if functional bulk is needed, a decision "based on an assessment of the strength deficit." Adjustments (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317):
- Include "very specific SPP-type exercises during the GPP either to rehabilitate any existing injuries or to eliminate any structural or functional deficiencies or imbalances."
- "curtail or eliminate standard types of GPP" for an advanced athlete or anyone who has trained regularly for a long time; GPP methods are "unsuitable for adequately or timeously stimulating improvements in performance among advanced athletes, whose trainability has already waned."
- GPP-type exercises "may be appropriate for brief periods during the SPP to facilitate recovery or prevent stagnation."
- In transition phases, "be careful not to allow prolonged GPP type training ... to diminish the sport specific fitness of the athlete" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).

Traditional schemes run GPP at high volume and low intensity, then shift to SPP with falling volume, rising intensity and growing emphasis on sport-specific qualities (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, Fig 6.1).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for curtailing GPP is waning trainability in advanced athletes, "whose continued growth depends on more specific or demanding methods" (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317). No further mechanism is given.

**When to apply** — When an experienced athlete's off-season still opens with weeks of generic conditioning, or when a returning athlete needs targeted corrective work early. Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline notes this line was "Not claimed in the interview"). The authors' advanced-athlete rule points the same way.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a case against GPP for novices or young athletes; the curtailment applies to advanced or long-trained athletes. The hypertrophy-phase decision rests on the strength-deficit assessment from Chapter 1, which carries its own contested status ([[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]]). Bondarchuk's transfer work sets general-preparation length by the sports-form cycle ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]]); Inference: that is a duration rule, compatible with this one.

**Example** — The authors' own cases: SPP-type rehabilitation exercises inside the GPP for an injured athlete, and brief GPP-type work inside the SPP to aid recovery (PDF p. 328 / printed p. 317).

# In-Season Stabilisation: About Twice a Week, No More Than 30 Minutes, a Few Multi-Joint Lifts

**What it is** — "Near the beginning of the competitive season, a *stabilisation phase* may be commenced to ensure that the various fitness qualities developed in the off-season are maintained throughout the season. It is important to remember that the average athlete usually has little desire to spend hours in a gymnasium or undertaking 'cross training'. Consequently, it is often recommended that stabilisation training generally needs to occupy a short period before or during practice or preferably twice a week for no more than 30 minutes in a gymnasium, using a limited number of major multi-joint exercises. Some of the basic strengthening and flexibility exercises may be integrated into normal practice sessions, using partners to offer resistance, if necessary" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is adherence: the average athlete "has little desire to spend hours in a gymnasium." They give no physiological basis for the twice-weekly, 30-minute dose; it is introduced as "often recommended."

**When to apply** — Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds that the line was "Not claimed in the interview" and that "The in-season dose itself is unknown"). Inference: the authors' twice a week, under 30 minutes, few multi-joint lifts is a concrete starting dose for that gap, and it fits the baseline's game week of a Monday heavy lift and a lighter Wednesday lift (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)).

**When NOT to apply** — The passage gives frequency and duration but no intensity, so it does not by itself say whether heavy loads are kept in season. It is framed for "the average athlete"; the authors do not say it suffices for elite or strength-power specialists. Elsewhere the book warns that prolonged heavy strength volume can impair speed-strength and technique ([[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]]), which argues for keeping the dose small but is a separate point.

**Example** — Inference: two 25-minute in-season sessions per week of trap-bar deadlift, front squat and bench press, plus partner-resisted strengthening during practice warm-ups, would fall inside the authors' description.

# The Rule of Sixty Percent: A Light Day or Week Carries About 60% of a Heavy One's Volume

**What it is** — "The *gradual overload principle*, with periodic underloading days or microcycles, is constantly adhered to through all training cycles to ensure that an adequate, but not excessive, training stimulus is imposed on the body. A preliminary recommendation is that individual workouts should generally be alternated in terms of light, medium and heavy loading to guard against overtraining and to ensure optimal training and competitive efficiency. This variation in training load on a daily, microcyclic and mesocyclic basis is essential for avoiding stagnation. In this respect, it is common to observe the well-known empirical *Rule of Sixty Percent*, which states that the training volume of any stage (day or microcycle) with light loading should be approximately 60% of the volume of a stage with heavy (maximal or near-maximal) loading" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors call it "empirical" and give no mechanism or source. The surrounding rationale is guarding against overtraining and stagnation.

**When to apply** — When writing a light day or deload week and needing a default size for it relative to the heavy unit. Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the rule gives one number for the "low" week in that wave.

**When NOT to apply** — It specifies volume only; the page says nothing about whether intensity also drops on the light stage. The rule is not tested on this page and no population is named. The authors give no figure for a "medium" stage. Inference: in Vorobyev's printed weekly distributions on PDF p. 333 the lightest week is well under 60% of the heaviest (for example 15% versus 37% of a month's load in Fig 6.3A, about 41%), so the book's own examples do not all follow the rule.

**Example** — Inference: if a heavy microcycle totals 20,000 kg of squat and pull volume, the rule puts the following light microcycle at about 12,000 kg.

**Related** — [[claim--heavy-medium-light-alternation-beats-monotonic-increasing-loading]], [[case-study--vorobyev-ermakov-weightlifting-load-distributions]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]]

# Track Reliability of Technique, and Progress Only When It Has Stabilised at 70-80% or Better

**What it is** — "Even the most meticulous computation and prescription of load intensity, volume and sequencing ... is of little consequence to performance if changes in technical mastery are not constantly monitored." Lab tests "simply identify the potential offered by the athlete's work capacity and not functional preparedness" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image). The tool is *reliability of technique*: the percentage of successes in executing the same specific skills, kept separately for training and competition. "A low competitive reliability relative to training reliability indicates that the athlete probably has difficulty in performing under conditions of high emotional excitement and needs to simulate those conditions during training"; "gym lifters" lift much more in training than on the platform, where emotional stress affects "not ... the obviously adequate levels of strength or power, but ... the technical skills required." Rule: "Progression to more difficult skills should not occur until the reliability at the preceding level of complexity or intensity has stabilised at a level of at least 70-80%," the "*zone-by-zone mastering of intensity* (Matveyev, 1977)." Technical-training dose is steered by a *feedforward method* ("the quantitatively planned long-term scheme") and a *feedback method* ("the ad hoc daily approach") because technical emphasis "can fluctuate rapidly" (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: performance depends on "functional preparedness, which relies on the mastery of specific motor skills," and "loss of form is prematurely attributed to overtraining or deficient training" when the real problem is inadequate monitoring and cyclical variation of skills training (PDF p. 329-330 / printed p. 318-319).

**When to apply** — Any skill progression with a clear success criterion (a lift made, a drill rep executed to standard). Eric's baseline: "Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time" (line 94) concerns physical qualities, not skill; Inference: the baseline has no explicit technique-reliability metric, so this is a gap the passage could fill. The authors later add a coach-scored Rating of Technique column to the session log (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The 70-80% threshold has no cited data beyond the Matveyev label, and it needs "zones of intensity or complexity" to be "formally laid down for each aspect of a given sport" first. Inference: in open, reactive team-sport skills a success rate is harder to define than in a weightlifting attempt, so the threshold transfers best to closed skills. The third bullet in the source list ("the premature introduction of skills") reads as a factor to avoid, not one to stress; the source wording is ambiguous.

**Example** — The authors' own: the "gym lifter" whose training lifts far exceed platform lifts, read as a technical and emotional problem rather than a strength deficit (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).

**Related** — [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]

# Eight Weaknesses of the Western "Modified Matveyev" Wave Model

**What it is** — Western texts give "the impression that there is solely one model of periodisation," usually Fig 6.1, "the scheme that increases training intensity and decreases volume smoothly as the year progresses (Matveyev, 1964)," aiming at "maximum intensity shortly before the main competition" (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319, verified against the page image). Fig 6.1 shows volume falling and intensity rising through the preparation phase and first transition phase (TF1, "during which intensive loading replaces extensive loading"), crossing before the competition phase, with a separate technique curve rising to a plateau in the competition phase; TF2 is "off-season restoration." The authors say this model "is suitable for certain sports for less qualified athletes," but "neither the only periodisation scheme nor the most applicable in all situations," and that many problems "have more to do with limited Western access to the author's original material than with the model itself." Their list (PDF p. 330-331 / printed p. 319-320, verified against the page images):
1. Volume and intensity are shown as inversely related, but which exercises count is not deducible; and holding volume fixed while intensity rises "does not necessarily lead to overtraining or injury" (Medvedev, 1986, found it "one of the most favourable ways of enhancing performance" past a certain level).
2. The smooth curves suit novices but need modification for advanced athletes.
3. One set of graphs implies every training means follows the same curve, though components interact (running stress "can seriously impair" strength work).
4. High initial volume, even at low intensity, may not be the best start for novices (soreness, impaired adaptation, reduced motivation).
5. The graphs say nothing about which fitness qualities make up the load; "The conjugate sequence model proposed by Verkhoshansky discussed later addresses" this.
6. They ignore exercise order and interaction.
7. They imply one peak per season, "rarely the case, especially in team sports."
8. Technique emphasis rises gradually, but "Beginners characteristically need far more emphasis on technical training and elite athletes far less."

Voice: item 5 names Verkhoshansky in the third person, so that sentence is Siff writing; the rest of the list reads as the authors' joint text.

**Why it works** — Each item carries its own reason (above). The overarching reason is that a single smooth graph hides content, interaction and individual level.

**When to apply** — When a plan is built by drawing one volume curve and one intensity curve for the whole year. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)); item 7 is the direct reason a single-peak curve does not fit. Also line 106 (undulating over strict linear progression, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)) fits items 1 and 2.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors accept the model for "less qualified athletes" in "certain sports," and they say the critique targets the Western "modified" version, not necessarily Matveyev. Evans's course presents classical Matveyev as non-linear, with wave fluctuations at daily, micro and mesocycle level ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]); Inference: that agrees with the authors' point that the Western smooth version misrepresents the original, not with the smooth version itself. Item 8 (beginners need more technique) sits against nothing on these pages but is stated without data.

**Example** — The authors' own: a middle-distance runner doing running and weight training at the same time, where demanding distance work or sprints "can seriously impair one's capabilities in many strength exercises," which a single strength-load curve cannot show (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319).

# Sporting Form Cannot Be Held Permanently, So Plans Must Change: Matveyev's Own Answer, and His Intermediate Mesocycle

**What it is** — The authors report that Matveyev "himself discussed some of the limitations and scope of his model" (Matveyev, 1981). He quotes Jim Ryun's periodised plan to show how Ryun "planned the individual aerobic and non-aerobic components of the microcycles and mesocycles which lead to achieving several world records in the same period" (PDF p. 331 / printed p. 320, verified against the page image). In commentary on that plan Matveyev stresses the *intermediate mesocycle*: similar to a transition cycle but "not at all transitional in nature," vital "in between a series of demanding competitions," going "further than being a mere maintenance phase, by also providing relative unloading and restoration in the form of specific active rest and even stimulating further development of some fitness qualities." Such phases should not be "monotonous, highly deterministic routines," should "allow the athlete wide freedom of personal choice of activities and encourage a positive emotional atmosphere," and may use GPP methods. Matveyev then asks: "Why not retain sporting form permanently as a state which is optimal for the athlete?" He answers that "the same training stressors which contribute positively to an athlete's fitness over a certain period can become negative stressors if used for too long, since adaptation is a characteristic of all life and variety ensures growth," and that "sporting form which may be optimal for a given stage of performance is not optimal for the next stage." The authors draw the conclusion: "the need for regular updating of any periodisation or organisational training model or even changing to another one which may differ radically" (PDF p. 331 / printed p. 320).

**Why it works** — Matveyev's reasons as reported: prolonged identical stressors turn negative, and the next performance level needs "further different adaptive reconstruction of all systems of the body" (PDF p. 331 / printed p. 320). No further mechanism is given.

**When to apply** — Between clusters of competitions, and when a plan that worked one year is being copied unchanged into the next. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract ... then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)); and bye weeks with "extra rest and recovery" plus "a speed and strength top-up" (line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)). Inference: a bye week is close to Matveyev's intermediate mesocycle in miniature: unloading plus some development, not pure rest.

**When NOT to apply** — The page reports Matveyev second-hand; the authors give no outcome data for intermediate mesocycles. The Ryun plan (Fig 6.2, PDF p. 332) is a single elite middle-distance runner; its structure does not transfer as a template to other sports (Inference). Note the book's figure numbering: two different figures on PDF p. 332 and p. 333 are both captioned "Figure 6.2."

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 6.2 (PDF p. 332 / printed p. 321, verified against the page image), "based on Matveyev, 1978," shows Ryun's season as a one-microcycle opening block, a four-microcycle competitive mesocycle, a two-microcycle intermediate ("INTERM") mesocycle, then a second four-microcycle competitive mesocycle. Total training distance (bars, km) is highest, about 170 km, in the opening block and the first intermediate microcycle, and falls to under about 50 km late in each competitive mesocycle; the mainly-aerobic and aerobic-anaerobic shares are small parts of each bar. The result line above marks races (2 mile, 1 mile, 880 yds, 1 mile relay, 1 mile) at about 97-100% with world-record dots. Values read by eye from the image.

# Six Broad Periodisation Schemes: Wave, Step, Equal Distribution, Pyramid, Concentrated, Pendulum

**What it is** — "there is not simply one grand unified model of periodisation, but several broad periodisation schemes, each with its own variations for different sports and different levels of athlete qualification" (PDF p. 332 / printed p. 321, verified against the page image):
1. *Smooth wave-like variations of the load over definite phases* (Matveyev 1977; Ozolin 1970; Sholikh 1966). "Research indicates that the load volume during the competitive phase should be about 10-15% lower than the maximum that is reached during the preparatory phase."
2. *Discontinuous step-like alternation of loads of different intensity* (light, medium, heavy), applied monotonically ("75-75%, 85-85%, 90-90%, 100-100%, 105-105%" of 1RM) or fluctuating ("85-85%, 90-90%, 100-100%, 95-95%..."), with load varied sharply session to session and across weeks and months (Figs 6.2-6.6); "corroborated" by Yakovlev 1971, Grokin 1951, Vorobyev 1972, Ermakov 1974.
3. *Equal distribution of training loads comprising strength and technical skills work* (Komarova 1984), used for the Soviet track-and-field team for the 1980 Olympics (Bondarchuk 1976, 1979). In one variant, large technique volume in the preparatory phase, greater strength volume near its end and early in competition: "Increase in strength without concurrent improvement in sport-specific skills training is considered inefficient."
4. *Asymmetric pyramid-like variation* (e.g. Reding 1971): load rises and falls with an upward trend, e.g. "80-90-95-100-95-90-100-105%."
5. *Wave-like concentration of loading with a given primary emphasis for about 5-8 weeks at a time* (Verkhoshansky 1978, 1979), each block the foundation for the next, "intended for more highly qualified athletes" and to be "prescribed intelligently to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 332-333 / printed p. 321-322).
6. *The pendulum approach* (Arosiev and others): "smooth, uniform, rhythmical alternation of the different components of training (e.g. strength, strength-speed, strength-endurance)" (PDF p. 333 / printed p. 322).

The next page says "The largest emphasis of this chapter will be on system 4, since the other more familiar systems have been discussed in depth in the references cited" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — A classification; the authors give per-scheme support only as citations (above). Voice: scheme 5 cites Verkhoshansky in the third person, so that item is Siff writing.

**When to apply** — When choosing or describing a model, name which of the six it is rather than "periodised." Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: that is closest to scheme 2 in its fluctuating form.

**When NOT to apply** — "System 4" is printed as the chapter's main emphasis, but system 4 is the asymmetric pyramid and the chapter's later sections and earlier pointer ("see 6.10") concern concentrated loading, which is system 5; Inference: probably a misnumbering, so treat the sentence as unclear. The "10-15% lower" competitive volume is attributed to "Research" via Matveyev 1964 with no data on the page. Scheme 5 is the concentrated-unidirectional model that Issurin 2016 judged insufficiently supported for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]; see [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]). The authors give no evidence for the pendulum approach.

**Example** — The authors' own: monotonic step loading at 75%, 85%, 90%, 100%, 105% of 1RM, each repeated (PDF p. 332 / printed p. 321). Inference: 105% assumes the 1RM used is an older or estimated one that the athlete now exceeds; the page does not explain it.

**What it is** — Figures illustrating step-like load alternation in weightlifting (PDF p. 333-334 / printed p. 322-323, all verified against the page images; the authors refer to them as "Figs 6.2-6.6" under scheme 2, PDF p. 332):

A, "the average week a few months before competitions": day 1 42%, day 2 23%, day 3 35% of the weekly load. B, "the week directly before a contest": 54%, 30%, 16%. Printed values.
- **Weekly volume within a month** (Fig 6.3, Vorobyev 1978). A, "highly qualified lifter in the month before a contest": weeks 1-4 at 15%, 23%, 37%, 25% of the monthly load. B, "if the previous month volume of loading was high": 13%, 21%, 30%, 36%. Printed values.

- **Two months, elite weightlifters** (Fig 6.5, Vorobyev 1978): L, M, L, S, M, L, M, L; "more effective than that of Figure 6.3, since world-class competitors can tolerate significantly larger loads."
- **Two months, well trained lifters "who can tolerate two successive weeks of heavy loading"** (Fig 6.6, Vorobyev 1978): L, L, S, M, L, L, S, M.

# Calculating Volume, Mean Intensity and Relative Intensity, and Why Averages Mislead

**What it is** — Volume is "intended to provide some measure of the total work done over a given period and intensity is a measure of the average force exerted"; approximate measures replace "the precise methods of physics" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323, verified against the page image).
- **Volume** of an exercise (kg) = weight x repetitions; workout volume = sum over "all the major exercises."
- **Number of lifts** = total repetitions.
- **Intensity** of an exercise = its volume / its repetitions; workout intensity = total volume / total lifts, "the average weight lifted."
- **Relative intensity** = intensity / 1RM x 100, "usually more meaningful."
- Exclusions: "Some authorities (Chernyak, 1978) stipulate that only weights of greater than 40% of 1RM should be taken into account ... since the strengthening effects of lighter weights than this is minimal." Then: "Generally, except for beginners, warmup sets with loads of less than about 70% of 1RM are not included in the calculations."
- Near-misses count: "if a weightlifter manages to raise a snatch or jerk above the head, but fails to complete the lift, then the attempt is counted" (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324).
- Hybrid exercises (e.g. 100 kg power clean x2 + front squat x3 + push press x1) are written as 100 over 2+3+1, volume 600 kg (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, verified against the page image).
- Some, such as Medvedev (1989), prefer number of lifts alone, since computed averages let "a few sets of lighter loads ... swamp the effect of a small number of maximal efforts" (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325).

**Why it works** — The authors' warning about averages: "the use of overall averages can be very misleading in prescribing training, since they give no indication of the range of loads used ... Thus, the overall demands of training must always be examined simultaneously in terms of intensity and volume" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323).

**When to apply** — Any weight-room load log or dashboard that reports tonnage or average load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)); the baseline adds an Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes." Inference: the same caveat applies to relative intensity computed here.

**When NOT to apply** — Two exclusion thresholds sit on the same page and are not reconciled: Chernyak's "greater than 40% of 1RM" and the general "less than about 70% of 1RM" warm-up exclusion; the worked example drops a 50% set as a warm-up, which follows the 70% rule. Record which rule a log uses. The method covers barbell lifts; the authors log jumps separately by height and repetitions (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325). Small-muscle exercises are usually excluded, but the authors warn this can hide fatigue (PDF p. 340; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Exercise A, 60 kg x 10, 80 kg x 8, 100 kg x 4, 110 kg x 2, 1RM 120 kg. The 60 kg set (50%) is dropped as a warm-up. Volume = 640 + 400 + 220 = 1260 kg; reps = 14; intensity = 1260 / 14 = 90 kg; relative intensity = 90 / 120 x 100 = 75%. Yet the top set was 110 kg (92%), and "The same relative intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions," which "would be far less demanding" (PDF p. 334 / printed p. 323). Inference: 3 x 3 at 75 kg is 62.5% of 120 kg, not 75%; the sentence only works if it means 90 kg, so treat that comparison as a printing slip.

**Related** — [[framework--intensity-zone-distribution-and-load-recording]], [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--intensity-defines-target-volume-defines-depth]]

# Record the Distribution of Lifts Across Intensity Zones, Not Just Volume and Mean Intensity

**What it is** — Because averages hide the range of loads, "it is preferable to determine the distribution of loading in different intensity zones. In strength sports, nine intensity zones are usually defined, although it is adequate to use the following five zones: 50%+ (50-59%), 60%+ (between 60-69%), 70%+ (70-79%), 80%+ (80-89%), 90%+ (90-100%)." The number or percentage of lifts in each zone is recorded with volume and intensity (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324, verified against the page image). Fig 6.7 (based on Matveyev 1977) plots number of lifts as a percentage of monthly volume across zones I-V: A, a "normal" distribution peaking at zone III at about 40%; B, skewed toward lower intensity, peaking at about 40% around zone II; C, skewed toward higher intensity, peaking at about 40% around zone IV (values read by eye). The training diary puts exercises, sets, reps and load on the left page and calculations on the right (Table 6.1: zone columns I-V, then Vol, NL, Iav, 1RM, Irel). These figures are recorded "at the level of the individual session, the week or microcycle, the month, the mesocycle and the macrocycle." Three notations for sets are given, e.g. "60 x 10, 70 x 8, 80 x 6, 80 x 6" or "10(60)1, 8(70)1, 6(80)2" (PDF p. 335-336 / printed p. 324-325).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that zone counts give "a clear visual overview of how the loading is imposed," which volume and mean intensity cannot (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324). They add a caution, not a mechanism: "The mistake should not be made of assuming that higher intensities (mean loads) or a greater number of lifts in the higher intensity zones will produce superior results. At any given time, there is an optimal load and load distribution for athletes of different bodymass and level of qualification, as well as individual responses to different loading regimes."

# Vorobyev's Mean Training Weight by Bodymass and Qualification, and Dvorkin's Junior Load Bands

**What it is** — For Olympic weightlifters, "based on research and experience with Russian lifters (Vorobyev, 1985)," the authors say "There is an optimal mean training weight in each bodymass division for each level of qualification (Table 6.2)." Two sentences later the same table "furnishes upper limits of the mean intensity which the speed-strength athlete should not exceed over any cycle of training" (PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325, verified against the page image). The values rise with qualification and bodymass, for example (mean training load, kg; Class III / Class II / Class I / CMS / MS):
- 52 kg: 51.0 / 63.5 / 70.0 / 78.0 / 80.0
- 75 kg: 70.0 / 92.0 / 99.0 / 111.0 / 116.0
- 100 kg: 82.0 / 101.0 / 113.0 / 125.0 / 132.0
- +110 kg: 86.0 / 109.0 / 120.0 / 130.0 / 147.0

(CMS = Candidate for Master of Sport, MS = Master of Sport.) The authors say the values rise as human strength increases, adjustable "by using the formula presented in Section 3.3.9." For juniors, Dvorkin's research (1980), using a maximum and recovery heart rate method, gives "fundamental training weights" of "50-70%" for 13-14 year olds, "60-90%" for 15-16 year olds and "80-90%" for 17-20 year olds, "the most suitable value depending on individual responses to the loading (Medvedev, 1986)."

**Why it works** — No mechanism; the table summarises Russian research and experience. The authors note that it "does not reflect the distribution of loading over the different intensity zones."

**When to apply** — As a reference for how much mean training load scales with qualification inside one bodymass class, and as an argument for setting load caps by level rather than by a single percentage. Eric's baseline: Prilepin's chart as the default rep/set guide (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: Table 6.2 is in absolute kilograms for weightlifting classes, so it does not convert to Baylor athletes; its use is the principle that mean load caps rise with qualification.

**When NOT to apply** — The table is introduced as both an "optimal" mean and an "upper limit" not to exceed; the source does not reconcile the two readings, so do not treat the numbers as targets. The junior percentages have no stated reference (percent of what maximum) on the page; Inference: probably of 1RM. Bondarchuk reports that model characteristics by qualification exist and are published in tables ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]]); that agrees in kind but is a separate data set.

**Example** — The authors' own table: a 75 kg Class II lifter's mean training load is 92.0 kg, a 75 kg Master of Sport's is 116.0 kg (Table 6.2, PDF p. 336 / printed p. 325).

**Related** — [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[framework--intensity-zone-distribution-and-load-recording]], [[claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]]

# Drawing Up the Plan: Estimate 1RM Safely, Lay Out the Year, Work Backwards From Each Competition, Then Fill Down to the Session

**What it is** — The authors' planning sequence (PDF p. 337-339 / printed p. 326-328; pages 337 and 339 verified against the page images, page 338 read from the text layer only):
1. **1RM first.** Computations rest on "percentages of a 1RM (Russian approach) or number of kilograms above or below one's 1RM (Bulgarian approach)." For a complete novice, "it is preferable to regard the first few weeks as a pre-testing, initial transitional phase," and if an estimate is needed, "it is more rational to obtain such an estimation from one's 5RM or 6RM, using extrapolation tables or graphs" (PDF p. 337 / printed p. 326).
2. **Annual bar.** Express the macrocycle as a divided bar of phases (Fig 6.8: introductory, GPP, transition, SPP, transition, competitive, transition; lengths "merely indicate a sequence"). The introductory phase familiarises the athlete with the exercises and prepares for testing.
3. **Work backwards.** Turn the bar into a graphic calendar (Fig 6.9, "entirely hypothetical"); "Once the major and other competitions are filled in, you work backwards from each one of them to identify the most appropriate mesocycles and sketch in the approximate graphs with the desired trends in intensity and volume. Then, after the actual computations have been made at the more detailed sub-levels, the exact graphs are drawn in" (PDF p. 337 / printed p. 326).
4. **Mesocycle plan** of every training means (strength, running, sport, plyometrics, swimming, recreational) by day (Table 6.3), then the microcycle plan of daily volume and intensity (Fig 6.11), then the session detail in a zone table or a simpler sets-and-reps table. Restoration should be planned even if plans "do not always include a specific row" for it (PDF p. 338 / printed p. 327).

Two cautions close the section: "these still remain guidelines, not scientific computations that will ensure a precisely predetermined outcome," and splitting a day into "a series of interrelated training modules comprising only a very few exercises at a time can be a highly effective way of optimising adaptation, since this can enable one to work at a higher intensity with more adequate restoration" (PDF p. 338 / printed p. 327).

**Why it works** — The authors give reasons, not mechanisms: the novice pre-testing phase avoids "excessively demanding" 1RM efforts, and working backwards places mesocycles relative to the competitions they serve.

**When to apply** — Building Baylor annual plans. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). The authors' "guidelines, not scientific computations" matches the roadmap framing. On 1RM: the baseline's Prilepin line notes there is "no true 1RM testing (Q10)" (line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)); the authors' 5RM or 6RM estimate is the same kind of workaround.

**When NOT to apply** — The 5RM/6RM extrapolation relies on tables from "Ch 1.3" that this entry has not checked. Fig 6.9's curves are labelled hypothetical, so do not read them as a recommended shape. Section 6.3 reports Verkhoshansky's view that mechanically dividing the year into periods and mesocycles is unsuitable for elite athletes ([[claim--periodisation-controversy-verkhoshansky-vs-zheljazkov]]); the backwards-planning method is the classical one he criticises.

**Example** — Inference: for a Saturday-game football season, fill in game dates, the bye week and postseason first, then place mesocycles backwards from the November priority window (baseline line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)), then compute weekly lifting volumes.

**Related** — [[framework--matveyev-microcycle-and-mesocycle-types-and-sequences]], [[framework--intensity-zone-distribution-and-load-recording]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[heuristic--circuit-progression-load-prescription-and-novice-pre-testing]], [[heuristic--apre-skill-learning-6rm-pyramid-test-and-rm-muscle-testing]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]]

# Cybernetic Periodisation: Steer the Preplanned Scheme With RPE and a Rating of Technique

**What it is** — "The use of numerical computations as the sole descriptor of loading often overlooks ... the athlete's *subjective perception of the intensity and overall effects of the loading*." Bulgarian weightlifting answered this with a method "which required athletes always to train at a perceived maximum load" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328, verified against the page image). The proposal:
- Add an RPE column ("Rating of Perceived Effort") on a 1-3 (light, medium, heavy), 1-10, or "most popular" 1-5 scale. "You do not record an RPE for every repetition or exercise, but note it mentally in each set and use it to guide you in your next set. At the end of the workout, you then record only the RPE for the heaviest or most demanding sets."
- RPE "usually be used to identify any decrease rather than an increase in actual load."
- Add a coach-scored Rating of Technique (RT) for the most demanding efforts, with video if more validity is needed (Table 6.4).
- Plot intensities, volumes, actual performances and RPEs on the same axes over time.

"This modified form of periodisation may be known as *cybernetic periodisation*, since the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback obtained from the lifter's current performance state" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image), after Wiener (1948). "Traditional periodisation can often prove to be as limited as non-periodised training, since all loading is based upon a fixed original input." It is "a quantified extension of what may be termed intuitive training." The Bulgarian "method of maximum effort": if the top lift "felt very demanding, the lifter might decrease the load by 10kg and perform a few sets of no more than 2 repetitions with it, and then follow this with an increase of 5kg for another few single attempts." Two side rules: periodically include minor exercises (calf raises, elbow curls, lat pulldowns) in calculations, since excluding them "might disguise the fact that they are fatiguing some muscle groups," and avoid placing them randomly before major lifts; and use RPE and RT to adjust for heavy loading from the athlete's job, "most significant in the case of heavy manual labourers" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the athlete responds to any exercise in terms of how the load feels at any given moment or period, rather than mechanically according to some numerical computation" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328); and "Over-reliance on numerical computations ... is a major reason why some coaches tend to dismiss their relevance" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). Voice: the cybernetic-periodisation label and this section read as Siff's own contribution (Section 6.3 refers back to it as what "this textbook introduced," PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334); the book does not attribute it to Verkhoshansky.

**When to apply** — Whenever a percentage-based plan runs on projected rather than tested maxes. Eric's baseline: Prilepin's chart is the default rep/set guide, with the baseline's own Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: RPE-guided downward adjustment is the authors' safeguard for exactly that case. For hard practice days in football, the "normal daily job" point applies by analogy to practice load before a lift (Inference).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors advise RPE mainly to reduce load, not to push it up. The 10 kg down, 5 kg up rule is a Bulgarian elite weightlifting example, not a general prescription. This entry overlaps with the authors' APRE in 5.2.2, which adjusts load by repetitions achieved rather than by perception ([[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]]); the two are compatible but separate tools. Issurin maps workout load onto Borg RPE bands on a different scale ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]); do not mix the scales.

**Example** — The authors' own: a Bulgarian lifter whose maximum attempt feels very demanding drops 10 kg for a few sets of at most 2 reps, then adds 5 kg for a few singles (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

# Cybernetic Periodisation: Steer the Preplanned Scheme With RPE and a Rating of Technique

**What it is** — "The use of numerical computations as the sole descriptor of loading often overlooks ... the athlete's *subjective perception of the intensity and overall effects of the loading*." Bulgarian weightlifting answered this with a method "which required athletes always to train at a perceived maximum load" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328, verified against the page image). The proposal:
- Add an RPE column ("Rating of Perceived Effort") on a 1-3 (light, medium, heavy), 1-10, or "most popular" 1-5 scale. "You do not record an RPE for every repetition or exercise, but note it mentally in each set and use it to guide you in your next set. At the end of the workout, you then record only the RPE for the heaviest or most demanding sets."
- RPE "usually be used to identify any decrease rather than an increase in actual load."
- Add a coach-scored Rating of Technique (RT) for the most demanding efforts, with video if more validity is needed (Table 6.4).
- Plot intensities, volumes, actual performances and RPEs on the same axes over time.

"This modified form of periodisation may be known as *cybernetic periodisation*, since the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback obtained from the lifter's current performance state" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image), after Wiener (1948). "Traditional periodisation can often prove to be as limited as non-periodised training, since all loading is based upon a fixed original input." It is "a quantified extension of what may be termed intuitive training." The Bulgarian "method of maximum effort": if the top lift "felt very demanding, the lifter might decrease the load by 10kg and perform a few sets of no more than 2 repetitions with it, and then follow this with an increase of 5kg for another few single attempts." Two side rules: periodically include minor exercises (calf raises, elbow curls, lat pulldowns) in calculations, since excluding them "might disguise the fact that they are fatiguing some muscle groups," and avoid placing them randomly before major lifts; and use RPE and RT to adjust for heavy loading from the athlete's job, "most significant in the case of heavy manual labourers" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the athlete responds to any exercise in terms of how the load feels at any given moment or period, rather than mechanically according to some numerical computation" (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328); and "Over-reliance on numerical computations ... is a major reason why some coaches tend to dismiss their relevance" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). Voice: the cybernetic-periodisation label and this section read as Siff's own contribution (Section 6.3 refers back to it as what "this textbook introduced," PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334); the book does not attribute it to Verkhoshansky.

**When to apply** — Whenever a percentage-based plan runs on projected rather than tested maxes. Eric's baseline: Prilepin's chart is the default rep/set guide, with the baseline's own Inference that "with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: RPE-guided downward adjustment is the authors' safeguard for exactly that case. For hard practice days in football, the "normal daily job" point applies by analogy to practice load before a lift (Inference).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors advise RPE mainly to reduce load, not to push it up. The 10 kg down, 5 kg up rule is a Bulgarian elite weightlifting example, not a general prescription. This entry overlaps with the authors' APRE in 5.2.2, which adjusts load by repetitions achieved rather than by perception ([[framework--apre-autoregulating-progressive-resistance-exercise]]); the two are compatible but separate tools. Issurin maps workout load onto Borg RPE bands on a different scale ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]); do not mix the scales.

**Example** — The authors' own: a Bulgarian lifter whose maximum attempt feels very demanding drops 10 kg for a few sets of at most 2 reps, then adds 5 kg for a few singles (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

# Heart-Rate Work-Capacity Tests for Lifters: the Novik Squat Test and an Adapted PWC-170

**What it is** — Heart rate can show what load computations miss: "If the heart rate increases noticeably prior to the heavier or heaviest training loads in any session, it indicates the presence of significant levels of emotional arousal and a more demanding level of training intensity, even though the periodisation computations might indicate otherwise" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, verified against the page image). Measure HR before, immediately after, and each minute for 4 minutes after an exercise; for resistance training, take recovery HR after "repetition squats, cleans and bench press" rather than on a treadmill, "because of the effects such as local muscle ischaemia."
- **Novik squat test** (Novik et al, 1980, Olympic weightlifters): at the start of a cycle, find the 1RM squat; then do "one set of 3 repetitions of squats" at "85-90% of this 1RM," and measure HR "for a period lasting one minute." Repeat through the cycle: "If the immediate post-squatting and the post-one minute heart rates decrease, then work capacity has increased and loading may be increased" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).
- **Adapted PWC-170** (Karpman et al, 1982; Dvorkin, 1988), PDF p. 341 / printed p. 330, verified against the page image: with the 10RM load, rest about 5 minutes, do 5 reps, measure HR (F1); rest another 5 minutes, do 8-10 reps, measure HR (F2). PWC-170 = N1 + (N2 - N1)(170 - F1)/(F2 - F1), where N = 9.8 x W x R x D, and D is the bar distance as a fraction of lifter height H (Table 6.5). The squat "is far more commonly used." Table 6.5 values (concentric D / equivalent D for total work): full back squat 0.35 H / 0.60 H; half squat 0.22 / 0.37; bench press 0.28 / 0.56; squat clean 0.67 / 1.26; split clean 0.55 / 0.77; clean pull 0.50 / 0.50; snatch pull 0.59 / 0.59; power clean 0.65 / 0.69; deep good morning 0.35 / 0.52; jerk from chest 0.54 / 0.60; split snatch 0.67 / 0.89.

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: a lower HR response to the same submaximal squat effort means higher work capacity (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329). No physiological explanation beyond that is given.

**When to apply** — As a low-cost in-house readiness and capacity check during a strength block, using an exercise athletes already do. Inference: Baylor's force-plate and GPS monitoring does not cover a lift-specific HR response, so the Novik test would be an addition, not a replacement.

**When NOT to apply** — The Novik test requires a measured 1RM squat, which the baseline says is not routinely tested (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material), citing Q10). Table 6.5 is not internally consistent with its own note: the text says eccentric action was "estimated to add 70% more work in each case where there is significant eccentric action," but the table's ratios differ (Inference from the printed values: back squat about +71%, bench press +100%, squat clean about +88%, power clean about +6%, pulls 0%). The book does not explain the variation. HR is also raised by "emotional arousal," so a high reading does not by itself separate fatigue from nerves.

**Example** — The authors' own: a weightlifter squats 3 reps at 85-90% of 1RM at intervals through a cycle; falling immediate and 1-minute post-set HR signals higher work capacity and permits more load (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329).

# Other Readiness Markers: Heart-Rate Modes, Morning Blood Pressure, the Coefficient of Effectiveness, and Palpation Soreness

**What it is** — Beyond the work-capacity tests, the authors list further markers (PDF p. 341-342 / printed p. 330-331, verified against the page images):
- **Heart-rate modes**: Cardiovascular HR Monitoring; Muscle Endurance HR Monitoring ("maintaining a heart rate of at least 80% of maximum is sometimes advocated during rowing training for Olympic rowers"); Postural HR Monitoring (resting HR versus HR immediately after and for a few minutes after "suddenly jumping up from a supine position"); Apnoeic HR Monitoring (before, during and after maximal breath holding, for weightlifting and wrestling); Medical HR Monitoring.

# Judging a Training Scheme by Order Analysis and Four Methods of Causal Analysis

**What it is** — To assess a training scheme from logged observations, the authors borrow "two distinct methods used for deriving information from experimental results or observations, namely *order analysis* and *causal analysis* (Siff, 1990)" (PDF p. 342-343 / printed p. 331-332, verified against the page images):
1. **Order analysis** "compares similarities and dissimilarities between items": compare a poorly known system with one "whose effects have been well established by experiment or by practice," or tabulate a system's variables to "deduce relationships or missing links" (examples: Mendeleev's periodic table, biological classification).
2. **Causal analysis**:
   - *Method of agreement*: if all conditions producing an outcome share one factor, it "may be the cause"; "It is usually difficult to ascertain that this is the only common cause."
   - *Method of difference*: two otherwise identical schemes differ in one factor; "The problem is that it is impossible to implement two identical training schemes."
   - *Method of concomitant variation*: a factor whose magnitude co-varies with the outcome "may be the cause"; "a causal relationship, but not a proof, is indicated," and the relation may be "positive or negative, linear or non-linear, direct or inverse."
   - *Method of residues*: once known causes and effects are removed, any residue is due to the remaining variable; it "faces the problem of handling isolated factors which may not be strictly independent."

The use: assessing "the merits of one of the many training exercises and regimes which are offered in textbooks, popular training magazines or seminars by various coaches" (PDF p. 343 / printed p. 332).

**Why it works** — The authors present these as "formal principles used in scientific research" applied as guidelines; each method's limitation is stated with it (above). Inference: the four causal methods correspond to Mill's methods of induction, which the book does not name.

**When to apply** — When a coach or vendor claims a new method works, or when reviewing why a team's block did or did not deliver. Inference: this pairs with the library's own review practice of checking which comparator a study used (for example Afonso et al. 2019's point about periodised-versus-constant comparisons, [[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]]).

**When NOT to apply** — These methods suggest causes, they do not prove them; the authors say so for concomitant variation and the method of difference. They are not a substitute for controlled studies where those exist (Inference).

**Example** — The authors' own illustration of residues: "if we notice that a change in training is not explainable by a change in training variable X or Y, then it may be due to change in yet another variable Z" (PDF p. 343 / printed p. 332).

**Related** — [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]], [[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]]

# Chernyak's Weekly Volume-Intensity Combinations for Strength-Speed Sports (Contested Inside the Book)

**What it is** — "Studies have shown that, in the annual macrocycle, the weekly levels of volume and intensity coincide fairly closely in sports requiring strength (Chernyak et al, 1979). Generally, the largest number of weeks involve medium volume and medium intensity, as well as weeks with high volume and high intensity." Chernyak's recommendations for strength-speed sports (PDF p. 343 / printed p. 332, verified against the page image):
1. "It is inadvisable always to combine low volume with low intensity, medium volume with medium intensity and large volume with high intensity."
2. "Training is most effective and least injurious if": medium volume, medium intensity "used most frequently (about 12-15 weeks per year)"; medium or high volume, low intensity next (9-10 weeks); low volume, medium intensity next (6-7 weeks).
3. Less often still: large volume, medium intensity (3-4 weeks); large volume, high intensity (2-3 weeks); low volume, high intensity (3-4 weeks); low volume, low intensity (1-2 weeks).

The authors add that overall volume and intensity "tell us little about the loading imposed in different intensity zones or at the level of individual muscle groups," nor about "the individual's perceived response," so attention must go to these and to "the level of mastery of the athlete" (PDF p. 343-344 / printed p. 332-333).

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; the basis is Chernyak's research, summarised without data. Inference: rule 1's word "always" may mean "do not tie volume to intensity in lockstep," which would make it a rule against rigid coupling rather than against medium/medium weeks.

**When to apply** — As a rough annual budget of week types for strength-speed athletes: mostly medium/medium, then higher-volume low-intensity, then low-volume medium-intensity, with high-intensity weeks rare. Eric's baseline: "In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 181, Inferred (transcript)), and "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). # The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; pages 344 and 345 verified against the page images, 346 read from the text layer) is written by Siff: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to "this textbook." It has three voices.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (citing Horwill 1992, 1995; Tschiene 1991, 1992). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).

**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).

**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. Evans frames the same split as "classic" versus "non-classic" literature ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Verkhoshansky's claim that British middle-distance runners won Olympic gold before, not after, adopting Matveyev's scheme widely after 1980, against Zheljazkov's reply that "all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

# The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; pages 344 and 345 verified against the page images, 346 read from the text layer) is written by Siff: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to "this textbook." It has three voices.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (citing Horwill 1992, 1995; Tschiene 1991, 1992). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).

**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).

**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. Evans frames the same split as "classic" versus "non-classic" literature ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Verkhoshansky's claim that British middle-distance runners won Olympic gold before, not after, adopting Matveyev's scheme widely after 1980, against Zheljazkov's reply that "all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

Section 6.3 reports critics of "the artificiality and clumsiness of classifying the various microcycles and mesocycles" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). Issurin's microcycle typology differs in names and in its load-wave detail ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); do not mix the two vocabularies without saying which is meant.

14	# Record the Distribution of Lifts Across Intensity Zones, Not Just Volume and Mean Intensity
15	
16	**What it is** — Because averages hide the range of loads, "it is preferable to determine the distribution of loading in different intensity zones. In strength sports, nine intensity zones are usually defined, although it is adequate to use the following five zones: 50%+ (50-59%), 60%+ (between 60-69%), 70%+ (70-79%), 80%+ (80-89%), 90%+ (90-100%)." The number or percentage of lifts in each zone is recorded with volume and intensity (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324, verified against the page image). Fig 6.7 (based on Matveyev 1977) plots number of lifts as a percentage of monthly volume across zones I-V: A, a "normal" distribution peaking at zone III at about 40%; B, skewed toward lower intensity, peaking at about 40% around zone II; C, skewed toward higher intensity, peaking at about 40% around zone IV (values read by eye). The training diary puts exercises, sets, reps and load on the left page and calculations on the right (Table 6.1: zone columns I-V, then Vol, NL, Iav, 1RM, Irel). These figures are recorded "at the level of the individual session, the week or microcycle, the month, the mesocycle and the macrocycle." Three notations for sets are given, e.g. "60 x 10, 70 x 8, 80 x 6, 80 x 6" or "10(60)1, 8(70)1, 6(80)2" (PDF p. 335-336 / printed p. 324-325).
17	
18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that zone counts give "a clear visual overview of how the loading is imposed," which volume and mean intensity cannot (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324). They add a caution, not a mechanism: "The mistake should not be made of assuming that higher intensities (mean loads) or a greater number of lifts in the higher intensity zones will produce superior results. At any given time, there is an optimal load and load distribution for athletes of different bodymass and level of qualification, as well as individual responses to different loading regimes."
19	
20	**When to apply** — When building weight-room reports, report lifts per zone per week alongside tonnage. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: Prilepin's chart is itself organised by intensity zones, so zone counts are the natural way to check a block against it.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Zone I is defined two ways on the same page: the text says "50%+ (50-59%)," while Table 6.1's column I is headed "60%-" (PDF p. 335 / printed p. 324, image). Pick one and state it. Zone counts depend on a current 1RM; without true 1RM testing they rest on projected maxes (the Inference attached to baseline line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). The authors give no target distribution; Fig 6.7 shows shapes, not prescriptions.
23	
24	**Example** — Inference: a week of 60 squat lifts with 12 in zone III, 30 in zone IV and 18 in zone V would plot as a Fig 6.7 type C (skewed high) distribution; the authors would warn against assuming that is better than type A.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]
