14	# Track Reliability of Technique, and Progress Only When It Has Stabilised at 70-80% or Better
15	
16	**What it is** — "Even the most meticulous computation and prescription of load intensity, volume and sequencing ... is of little consequence to performance if changes in technical mastery are not constantly monitored." Lab tests "simply identify the potential offered by the athlete's work capacity and not functional preparedness" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318, verified against the page image). The tool is *reliability of technique*: the percentage of successes in executing the same specific skills, kept separately for training and competition. "A low competitive reliability relative to training reliability indicates that the athlete probably has difficulty in performing under conditions of high emotional excitement and needs to simulate those conditions during training"; "gym lifters" lift much more in training than on the platform, where emotional stress affects "not ... the obviously adequate levels of strength or power, but ... the technical skills required." Rule: "Progression to more difficult skills should not occur until the reliability at the preceding level of complexity or intensity has stabilised at a level of at least 70-80%," the "*zone-by-zone mastering of intensity* (Matveyev, 1977)." Technical-training dose is steered by a *feedforward method* ("the quantitatively planned long-term scheme") and a *feedback method* ("the ad hoc daily approach") because technical emphasis "can fluctuate rapidly" (PDF p. 330 / printed p. 319, verified against the page image).
17	
18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: performance depends on "functional preparedness, which relies on the mastery of specific motor skills," and "loss of form is prematurely attributed to overtraining or deficient training" when the real problem is inadequate monitoring and cyclical variation of skills training (PDF p. 329-330 / printed p. 318-319).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Any skill progression with a clear success criterion (a lift made, a drill rep executed to standard). Inference: `docs/method-baseline.md` records no explicit technique-reliability metric, so this is a gap the passage could fill. The authors later add a coach-scored Rating of Technique column to the session log (PDF p. 339 / printed p. 328; see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]).
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The 70-80% threshold has no cited data beyond the Matveyev label, and it needs "zones of intensity or complexity" to be "formally laid down for each aspect of a given sport" first. Inference: in open, reactive team-sport skills a success rate is harder to define than in a weightlifting attempt, so the threshold transfers best to closed skills. Inference: the third bullet in the source list ("the premature introduction of skills") reads as a factor to avoid, not one to stress; the source wording is ambiguous.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' own: the "gym lifter" whose training lifts far exceed platform lifts, read as a technical and emotional problem rather than a strength deficit (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]

Consequently, it is often recommended that stabilisation training generally needs to occupy a short period before or during practice or preferably twice a week for no more than 30 minutes in a gymnasium, using a limited number of major multi-joint exercises. 15	
16	**What it is** — "Some authorities consider that one of the transition phases should be recognised as a *conversion phase* during which specialised training converts maximum strength either into speed-strength or strength-endurance. 20	- **Macrocycle**: "a single competitive season," typically "10-12 months." A "large macrocycle" may mean the four years between Olympics or the years taken to move up one qualification Class.
21	- **Multi-year plan**: longer than an Olympic cycle, usually a career stage or whole competitive lifespan.
22	- Three conventional major phases: "preparation, competition and post-competition," with transition phases between them.
23	
24	Terminology warning: "earlier Russian literature, in contravention of the meaning of the prefixes meso- (middle) and macro- (large), used the term macrocycle to refer to what is now known as a mesocycle and vice versa"; this book uses the "linguistically corrected meanings" (PDF p. 327 / printed p. 316).
25	
26	**Why it works** — Definitional. The authors' design rule for every level: "The contents and characteristics of each cycle are determined by the specific goals or results desired at the end of the cycle," while avoiding units that develop abilities "which interfere with one another" or try to develop "too many or all types of fitness," which would contravene "the heterochronicity principle" (PDF p. 327 / printed p. 316).
27	
28	**When to apply** — When reading older Soviet sources, check which way they use meso and macro before comparing durations. Eric's baseline: "Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 179, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the authors' 5-10 day microcycle agrees with that reminder.
29	
30	**When NOT to apply** — The durations are typical ranges, not rules; the authors' own planning section later calls the microcycle "commonly a week long" (PDF p. 337 / printed p. 326), and Section 6.3 reports critics who object to fixing cycles at "an exact number of days or weeks" (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). The Bulgarian figure of more than 5 sessions a day applies to elite weightlifters and is not a general model (Inference).
31	
32	**Example** — The authors' own: a macrocycle of 10-12 months made of mesocycles of 1-4 months, each made of microcycles of 5-10 days, each containing at least two different types of workout (PDF p. 327 / printed p. 316).

18	2. "The maximum training benefits are derived by using muscle tension of no less than 40-50% of one's 1RM"
19	3. "Maximum training effect does not require prolonging muscle tension to the point of fatigue"
20	4. "One single maximal strength effort per day is sufficient to maintain progress"
21	
22	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the four points; they frame them within their summary of 1.16: each stimulus causes an acute and a delayed response, and supercompensation follows if intensity, duration, restoration and timing of the next stimulus are right (PDF p. 325 / printed p. 314).
23	
24	**When to apply** — As a historical anchor for two practical ideas: training to fatigue is not required for a strength effect (point 3), and brief maximal efforts can sustain progress (point 4). Eric's baseline: "Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days; a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 108, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: point 4 is consistent with a small retention dose, though Hettinger's statement concerns daily maintenance of progress, not a residual window.
25	
26	**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves say the points "have been modified and extended by more recent research," and they cite none of it here. Point 2's 40-50% of 1RM is a different figure from the Chapter 1 threshold of "roughly one-third of maximal strength" (Hettinger and Muller, 1953; [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]], PDF p. 33-34): the 1953 figure is a minimum threshold for any gain in an average person, the 1961 figure is the level for "maximum training benefits." Inference: so they answer different questions and are not a contradiction. The Chapter 1 entry also records that the needed intensity rises to 80-95% as the athlete adapts, so 40-50% is not a ceiling for trained athletes. Inference: much of Hettinger's work was isometric, and the page does not say whether "1RM" here was measured isometrically or dynamically.
27	
28	**Example** — Inference: a novice on a once-daily single near-maximal effort, stopping well short of fatigue, would satisfy all four points as listed; the book gives no worked example.
29	
30	**Related** — [[claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus]], [[claim--hettinger-muller-isometric-strength-gain-rate]], [[claim--seasonal-trainability-hettinger-muller-ultraviolet]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]]

lines: # The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

-**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; pages 344 and 345 verified against the page images, 346 read from the text layer) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.

+**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.
